title: Living there
hook: "abodes": a place to live all day, not only on the cushion

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was muditā, gladness at another's good fortune, with four rooms matched to whoever walks in. Your line: notice who just walked in.

Visiting a place isn't the same as living there. A weekend at a friend's cabin can feel wonderful. But you don't know the cabin until a rainy Tuesday, doing the dishes, in a bad mood. It's easy to treat kindness like that cabin: somewhere to visit during a quiet sit, before driving back to real life. The name the Buddha gave these four qualities says something else.
screen: `VISITING ISN'T LIVING.` → `A WEEKEND CABIN.` → `WHAT THE NAME SAYS.`

segments.voice: Twelve days ago, brahmavihara came apart into brahma, the sublime, and vihara, a dwelling, the same word used for a monastery, where monks actually live. Take that second half at its word. The name isn't four exercises. It's four homes. The Metta Sutta, a short discourse on kindness that Theravada monks and lay people chant, says it directly. After describing a mind of kindness toward all beings, it says to keep this mindfulness standing, walking, sitting or lying down, for as long as you're awake, and it calls that a sublime abiding, here and now. Standing, walking, sitting, lying down: that's the whole day. The bus stop, the grocery aisle, the moment before sleep. The cushion is where you learn the way home; it isn't the only place home exists. And a house you live in gets small repairs all the time. You notice the drip and fix it. Nobody lives in kindness perfectly. You notice you've wandered into irritation, and you come back, again and again, the way you come back to your own front door at the end of the day. In this picture, the aim isn't a special feeling during meditation. It's that, little by little, these four become the ordinary weather of a life.
screen: `VIHARA: A DWELLING.` · `STANDING, WALKING, SITTING, LYING DOWN.` · `THE CUSHION TEACHES THE WAY HOME.` · `SMALL REPAIRS, ALL DAY.` · then, large: `LIVE THERE.`

segments.voice: Picture your day ahead with four checkpoints, morning, midday, afternoon and evening, each one a single breath and one question: where am I living right now, in kindness, compassion, gladness, equanimity, or somewhere else? Try the first one now: one breath, no judging the answer. Just notice it, and turn toward home.
Living there. Vihara means a dwelling: the four immeasurables are homes to live in all day, not places to visit.
Your line: live there. The four are homes, not weekend cabins. That's two hundred forty-four days.

howItsDone: The Metta Sutta is chanted in Theravada monasteries and homes, and teachers encourage bringing kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity into ordinary activity, walking, working and talking, not only into formal sitting.

fork.setup: you felt deeply kind on the cushion this morning. an hour later you're snapping at a slow driver. what does the Metta Sutta's teaching suggest?
options: notice where you are, and come back home, right there in the car.
save kindness for the next sit.
fork.reveal: the sutta asks for kindness standing, walking, sitting, lying down: the car is part of the house.

original.note: Pali brahmavihāra: a sublime dwelling, a place to live, not just visit.

trapdoor: what you thought: brahmavihara is a fancy word for a meditation technique.
what it means: a sublime dwelling, a home you live in all day.

what a scholar hears: vihāra, from vi + harati, can mean a way of abiding, of spending one's time, and a monastic dwelling; the Metta Sutta calls this kindness a brahmavihāra, a sublime abiding, here and now.
recall: ill will, the wish for someone to suffer

notes: The Metta Sutta is paraphrased; confirm the 'standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as awake' line and 'sublime abiding here' are fairly rendered.
Etymology of vihāra (vi + √hṛ) and its two senses: confirm.
